body:
Oct 25, 2026 7:30pm PT	
	

			


			
			
	

									©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection
	

		
	
				

	“Obsession” led this year’s Fangoria Chainsaw Awards with the most amount of wins, taking home five awards including Best Director for Curry Barker and Best Lead Performance for Inde Navarrette.

	Celebrating achievements in horror film, television and gaming, the fan-voted awards premiered Sunday on Shudder and were hosted by Devon Sawa (“Final Destination,” “Chucky”). Among the night’s most stand-out moments were “Insidious” star Lin Shaye presenting the final award of the evening for “Obsession” and “Cujo” star Dee Wallace presenting the Goodest Boy award to the leading canine in “Good Boy,” Nova Scotia retriever Indy.
	

	“Like the genre it honors, the true fun of the Chainsaw Awards is that we have the audience’s permission to push the envelope. Horror fans not only want to celebrate the films and individuals who kept them watching, but they want to do it in a manner befitting the thing they love,” said Michael Varrati, who wrote and directed the ceremony. “That’s why we can present a special award to a dog who became a fan favorite or send our scream king host into a corn maze to contend with things lurking behind the rows.”


	“Backrooms” earned the second highest amount of Chainsaw Awards, receiving three wins for Best First Feature, Best Cinematography and Best Score. “Widow’s Bay” took home Best Series, while “Resident Evil: Requiem” won Best Video Game.

	Special honorees of the night include Joe Bird, (“Talk to Me,” “Leviticus”) who received the Editor’s Eyeball Award to recognize his rising career in horror. A second Editor’s Eyeball Award was presented to co-presenter James A. Janisse, honoring him and Chelsea Rebecca or creating the horror YouTube channel, “Dead Meat.”
	

	The ceremony was executive produced by Armen Aghaeian, Tara Ansley and Abhi Goel, with Amanda Grace Collins serving as lead producer and Phil Nobile Jr. and Varrati as producers.

title: From ‘Hoop Dreams’ to ‘Flee’: The 20 Documentaries That Deserved a Best Picture Oscar Nomination
description:
Oct 25, 2026 4:55pm PT	
	

	
		From ‘Hoop Dreams’ to ‘Flee’: The 20 Documentaries That Deserved a Best Picture Oscar Nomination
body:
Oct 25, 2026 4:55pm PT	
	

	
		From ‘Hoop Dreams’ to ‘Flee’: The 20 Documentaries That Deserved a Best Picture Oscar Nomination
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Getty / A24
	

		
	
				

	In nearly a century of Oscars, not a single documentary has been nominated for best picture. But that shouldn’t be the case.

	While a documentary can win its own Oscar, reshape the cultural conversation and become one of the defining films of its era, these nonfiction feature films have been excluded from the top category meant to honor the year’s best filmmaking. When the Academy expanded the Best Picture lineup from five to 10 after the snub of “The Dark Knight” (2008), the press release led with the possibility of a documentary getting recognized. That has yet to happen … perhaps until now?

	That assumption is finally being tested this season with “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s nonfiction sensation about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Acclaim and box office success are raising the possibility that a documentary could finally break one of the Academy’s longest-standing barriers. If it earns a nomination, the achievement would be historic. But it would also raise an uncomfortable question: Why did it take this long?

	To celebrate this potential historic nomination, Variety is ranking the 20 films that should have received a best picture nomination in the past 40 years.

	The films mentioned here span genres, styles and subjects, from the pursuit of an NBA dream to a high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers, from a confrontation with Indonesia’s history of mass killing to a real-time account of Edward Snowden’s revelations.

	You can blame the Academy at large for some of these omissions; others tie directly to the Documentary Branch itself, which snubbed many of them in its own category.

	If “You Can See Everything” finally breaks through, it will undoubtedly have earned its place in history. But it should not have been the first. Many others from this very year could also be deemed worthy, such as “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” and “Naza.”

	Read the list below.

	Honorable mentions: “An Inconvenient Truth” (2006); “Senna” (2010); “The Act of Killing” (2012); “Apollo 11″ (2019)


			
			
	Daughters (2024)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Sundance Institute				
					
				

	Angela Patton and Natalie Rae’s “Daughters” follows four girls preparing for a father-daughter dance inside a Washington, D.C., prison as part of a fatherhood program Patton helped build.

	The filmmakers’ choice to focus on the girls’ anticipation, anger and longing is its strongest element. It carries the film toward a dance sequence of almost unbearable tenderness.

	It won both the Audience Award and the Festival Favorite prize at Sundance, then made the documentary shortlist only to miss the nomination at the 2025 ceremony. Few films that year said more about love under impossible conditions.

		
			
			
	Man on Wire (2008)
			
								
				

	James Marsh’s “Man on Wire” reconstructs Philippe Petit’s 1974 high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers. Through interviews, archival footage and recreations, Marsh builds a structure as a model for any good movie heist.

	“Man on Wire” won the documentary Oscar at the 2009 ceremony, and its success lives on, demonstrating how effectively a nonfiction film could deliver the pleasures of a caper.

		
			
			
	O.J.: Made in America (2016)
			
										
					Image Credit: ESPN				
					
				

	There are strong feelings about whether or not Ezra Edelman’s Oscar winner is, in fact, a documentary feature, but it’s included nonetheless. 

	Edelman’s nearly eight-hour “O.J.: Made in America” is an expansive examination of race, celebrity, policing and the American justice system, using the life of O.J. Simpson as a lens through which to understand the country’s social and cultural divisions. What begins as a portrait of an athlete becomes a sweeping account of Los Angeles and the forces that shaped one of the most consequential public dramas of the modern era.

	The documentary feature Oscar winner’s format also exposed the boundaries of the category. Its recognition prompted renewed scrutiny of how the Academy treats multipart nonfiction projects, contributing to subsequent eligibility changes concerning episodic work.

	Whatever the debate over its classification, the filmmaking is extraordinary. Its scope exceeds that of most narrative features.

		
			
			
	Won’t You Be My Neighbor? (2018)
			
										
					Image Credit: Everett Collection / Everett Colllection				
					
				

	Morgan Neville’s portrait of television icon Fred Rogers became the highest-grossing biographical documentary of its time and became a sensation for all of us who grew up with the prolific figure.

	Rather than canonize its subject, Oscar winner Neville (“20 Feet From Stardom”) examines the radical patience behind “Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood” and the quiet conviction that children deserved to be taken seriously. 

	The film made the documentary shortlist but, shockingly, missed a nomination at the 2019 ceremony, a snub that still stings.

	Few films that year moved audiences so completely, in any category.

		
			
			
	Flee (2021)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Neon				
					
				

	Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s “Flee” uses animation to tell the story of Amin, an Afghan refugee who reveals the full extent of his childhood and his journey to safety. The decision to use the animation medium for the testimony allows Amin to revisit traumatic memories while preserving his anonymity, creating a visual language for experiences that would be difficult to reconstruct. 

	“Flee” made Oscar history by becoming the first film nominated for documentary feature, international feature and animated feature in the same year. It lost in all three categories, and best picture remained out of reach. 

	Rasmussen’s film is a reminder that nonfiction is not confined to one visual language or storytelling tradition. 

		
			
			
	The Look of Silence (2014)
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty				
					
				

	Many will argue I chose the wrong Joshua Oppenheimer film, and that “The Act of Killing” is more worthy of a spot than its companion piece. That a filmmaker’s work can spark such a debate is itself a mark of genius.

	“The Look of Silence” approaches Indonesia’s 1965-66 mass killings through an optometrist whose brother was murdered during the violence. Oppenheimer resists the conventions of a historical exposé, allowing pauses and glances to communicate what his subjects refuse to say. 

	The film landed a documentary feature nomination but lost to “Amy.” 

		
			
			
	Cameraperson (2016)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Sundance Film Festival				
					
				

	Kirsten Johnson spent decades as a documentary cinematographer, filming subjects in war zones, hospitals and interview rooms. With “Cameraperson,” she assembled fragments from that career into a moving essay about the ethics of looking and the emotional toll of bearing witness.

	The doc branch failed to nominate “Cameraperson,” a shocking omission for a work so widely admired for its originality. Johnson’s 2020 follow-up, “Dick Johnson Is Dead,” a playful and heartbreaking reckoning with her father’s decline, that could just as easily have claimed this spot.

		
			
			
	13th (2016)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Netflix				
					
				

	Ava DuVernay’s “13th” examines the connection between the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery, and the rise of mass incarceration in the United States. Through interviews with scholars, activists and politicians, alongside archival footage, DuVernay builds an argument about the enduring relationship between race and the criminal justice system.

	Rather than treating the amendment as a historical endpoint, she traces how its language became a blueprint for systems of control, and presenting a complex history with clarity and urgency.

	“13th” opened the 2016 New York Film Festival and landed a documentary feature nom, losing to “O.J.: Made in America.” 

	A decade later, DuVernay returned to NYFF with the equally urgent “14th,” the festival’s 2026 closing night film, which Netflix will also release.

		
			
			
	Dear Zachary: A Letter to a Son About His Father (2008)
			
								
				

	No documentary has made me cry more than the one about a baby named Zachary.

	Kurt Kuenne began “Dear Zachary” as a film for the infant son of his murdered best friend, Andrew Bagby. And what starts as a tribute built from home videos, photographs and memories becomes a devastating account of grief, family and a legal system that fails those seeking justice.

	Kuenne is not a detached observer. As events unfold, the film’s purpose changes, and its structure takes on a force no viewer can anticipate. Kuenne’s mid-film narration is something your heart can never properly prepare for.

	Nonetheless, the documentary branch passed on “Dear Zachary.” It remains one of the clearest examples of why documentaries deserve to be considered among the year’s best films, not merely the year’s best documentaries.

		
			
			
	Exit Through the Gift Shop (2010)
			
								
				

	Banksy’s “Exit Through the Gift Shop” makes uncertainty part of the moviewatching experience. 

	Is the film documenting an absurd art-world spectacle, manufacturing one or doing both at once? Banksy never provides a definitive answer, and the film’s refusal to settle the question gives it life.

	“Exit Through the Gift Shop” earned a documentary feature nom, losing to “Inside Job.” Moreover, it challenged the assumption that documentaries must present a distinction between observer and participant.

		
			
			
	I Am Not Your Negro (2016)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of TIFF				
					
				

	Raoul Peck’s Oscar-nominated “I Am Not Your Negro” takes James Baldwin’s unfinished manuscript about Medgar Evers, Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. and transforms it into a searing cinematic essay on race and America. 

	Samuel L. Jackson narrates Baldwin’s words, with the film’s force coming from the collision between the writer’s observations and a country that still refuses to reckon with its past. It’s sheer brilliance, and always timely.

		
			
			
	Three Identical Strangers (2018)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Sundance Film Festival				
					
				

	Tim Wardle’s film opens as a feel-good reunion of triplets separated at birth and curdles into an account of a secret psychological study that treated infants as test subjects. Wardle controls the revelations with the discipline of a thriller, letting each turn leave the viewer shocked before the next is revealed. 

	Like “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?,” it was shortlisted and then passed over entirely by the documentary branch. Its story of nature, nurture and institutional betrayal deserved a much wider stage.

		
			
			
	Citizenfour (2014)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of The Weinstein Company				
					
				

	Laura Poitras’ “Citizenfour” puts viewers inside a Hong Kong hotel room while Edward Snowden meets journalists and begins revealing classified information about government surveillance. Poitras allows conversations to develop in real time, building suspense through the simple act of watching history unfold.

	“Citizenfour” won the documentary Oscar at the 2015 ceremony, but no best picture heat would ensue. 

		
			
			
	Searching for Sugar Man (2012)
			
								
				

	Malik Bendjelloul’s “Searching for Sugar Man” chases the ghost of Rodriguez, a Detroit musician whose albums vanished in America but became anthems in apartheid-era South Africa, where fans knew nothing about the man behind the music. 

	By my estimation, it’s the single standout nonfiction film of its decade.

	Bendjelloul builds the mystery like a detective story, with an emotional payoff that feels almost too extraordinary to be true. Rodriguez’s incredible songs carry a story about fame, obscurity and the strange ways art outlives the circumstances of its making.

	Oscar voters handed it the documentary prize in 2013. Nobody mounted a best picture push for a film that had already proven it could hold a broad audience in its palm. Bendjelloul died in 2014 at 36, but the joyous discovery he left behind is well intact.

		
			
			
	Grizzly Man (2005)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Werner Herzog’s “Grizzly Man” begins with footage shot by Timothy Treadwell, a self-appointed protector of Alaskan grizzlies who was killed by one of the animals he sought to defend. Herzog’s narration becomes a film unto itself, challenging Treadwell’s romantic vision of the wilderness.

	The footage is funny, unnerving and devastating, sometimes within the same frame. Few filmmakers have turned a real-life tragedy into a philosophical inquiry so effectively without losing sight of the person at its center.

	Unfortunately, this was yet another victim of the doc branch’s allergy to mainstream and successful films, even though it’s widely considered among Herzog’s most celebrated works.

		
			
			
	Stories We Tell (2012)
			
										
					Image Credit: National Board of Canada				
					
				

	Sarah Polley’s “Stories We Tell” is an investigation into her own family history and becomes a remarkably intricate exploration of memory, and the fragile relationship between personal truth and the stories people preserve.

	Polley interviews relatives and friends, reconstructing family moments with its most effective moments being best experienced without advance knowledge of the revelations it shows.

	“Stories We Tell” was snubbed for the documentary Oscar, let alone best picture. That omission is particularly striking given Polley’s command of structure and her willingness to question the very conventions on which documentary filmmaking depends. 

		
			
			
	Bowling for Columbine (2002)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©United Artists/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Michael Moore turned the Columbine High School massacre into a mirror for America to see. 

	“Bowling for Columbine” interrogates America’s relationship with guns, violence and fear, mixing interviews, archival footage and Moore’s confrontational on-camera presence into an argument that dared audiences to fight back. 

	Few releases of 2002 commanded that attention.

	The Writers Guild made it the first documentary to win its original screenplay prize, and the Academy followed with the documentary Oscar, where Moore’s “shame on you, Mr. Bush” speech became the most talked-about moment of the night (and history).

		
			
			
	Hoop Dreams (1994)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Fine Line Features/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	No documentary snub remains quite as painful as the Academy’s failure to recognize Steve James’ “Hoop Dreams.”

	Over five years, James followed Chicago teenagers William Gates and Arthur Agee as they pursued basketball dreams that promised an escape from poverty. The result is a nearly three-hour American epic about race, class, family and the machinery that turns young athletes into commodities.

	Critics embraced the film as one of the year’s finest, regardless of genre. The Academy’s documentary branch, however, failed to nominate it, prompting widespread criticism and contributing to voting changes in the documentary nomination process. 

	Interestingly, “Hoop Dreams” managed to receive an Oscar nomination for film editing, but best picture was likely an even more distant possibility.

		
			
			
	The Thin Blue Line (1988)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Miramax Films				
					
				

	Errol Morris’ investigation into the 1976 killing of a Dallas police officer did something few doc films hope to do: It helped free an innocent man. 

	Randall Dale Adams was released from prison within a year of the film’s debut, after Morris’ interviews exposed the holes in the case against him.

	Its stylized reenactments, Philip Glass score and noir structure reinvented the nonfiction form in many ways.

	Once again, the doc branch had other plans, with a snub measured just as scandalous in its moment as “Hoop Dreams” would be six years later.

	Leaving out the film that changed how documentaries are made is indefensible.

		
			
			
	Paris is Burning (1990)
			
								
				

	Jennie Livingston’s “Paris Is Burning” documents Harlem’s ballroom scene in the late 1980s, where Black and Latino queer performers built houses, families and an entire vocabulary of survival in the face of poverty, racism and the AIDS crisis. 

	Its subjects, including Pepper LaBeija, Dorian Corey and Venus Xtravaganza, are among the most vivid figures nonfiction cinema has captured. 

	The film won the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance yet was snubbed by the Academy’s documentary branch at the 1992 ceremony. Decades later, its influence has been felt in artistic achievements such as television’s “Pose,” “RuPaul’s Drag Race” and the mainstream itself.

		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Director Lance Oppenheim Says Billy Evans ‘Didn’t Care About Being Seen Naked’; Evans Asked, ‘Want to Film Me Showering?’
description: “You Can See Everything” audiences were expecting to be taken aback for a variety of reasons when watching the documentary, but a full-frontal shot
body:
“You Can See Everything” audiences were expecting to be taken aback for a variety of reasons when watching the documentary, but a full-frontal shot of Elizabeth Holmes’ partner Billy Evans wasn’t something many foresaw experiencing in the theater. Lance Oppenheim, who co-directed the buzzy A24 doc with Nathan Fielder, has now revealed just how that jarring shower scene came to be — and why Evans might have been fine with revealing all to begin with. 
	

	“I honestly don’t know,” Oppnehim said when asked why Evans would agree to appear naked in a recent GQ interview. “It’s beyond me, but I’ve heard interesting theories that people have when they see it,” he said, before getting into the technical details of how they shot it. “There’s a camera in the bathroom, there’s a camera that was on Nathan, there’s a camera outside the bathroom, and there’s an interaction that we see after Billy leaves where he sort of looks at the camera and smiles.”


	“So I don’t know what that means, but I feel like there’s enough stuff in there that gives me the impression that maybe he was excited that people could see everything and that there was full access, I guess,” Oppenheim continued. “But it really beats me, honestly. We were in the car ride on the way back from the gym, and I said to Billy, ‘We will give you some time to shower.’ And Billy responded, ‘Want to film me showering?’ I offered to film him in a way that could avoid seeing his genitals, but Billy said he didn’t care about being seen naked.”

	Ahead of the film’s release earlier this month, Evans admitted he hadn’t seen the doc while appearing on the “All-In” podcast. “I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said on the podcast, admitting that Holmes “looks insane” in the trailer. 
	

	Before hitting theaters on Oct. 16, “You Can See Everything” had been quietly in the works from Fielder and Oppenheim for more than three years. The doc offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. 

	In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score.

	The film has been a major hit with audiences, bringing in $15.6 million from 855 theaters in its opening weekend (the best start for a nonmusical documentary in 20 years) and adding another $19.5 million after expanding to 2,655 venues for its sophomore outing.

title: Peggy King, ‘George Gobel Show’ Actress and Singer of the ’50s, Dies at 96
description: Peggy King, a 1950s television and recording star, died Sunday following a battle with Alzheimer’s at the Saunders House Assisted Living facility i
body:
Peggy King, a 1950s television and recording star, died Sunday following a battle with Alzheimer’s at the Saunders House Assisted Living facility in Wynnewood, Pa. She was 96.

	King’s publicist, Alan Eicher, confirmed her death. 

	King was a regular on the “George Gobel Show” from 1954-57. Gobel dubbed her “Pretty Perky Peggy King,” a nickname that stuck for the rest of her career. She was nominated for an Emmy Award for best female singer in 1955. She performed “Count Your Blessings” at the 1955 Academy Awards and co-hosted the Emmys in 1958.
	

	King appeared on shows including Bob Hope’s “Chevy Show,” “American Bandstand,” “The Steve Allen Show,” “The Kraft Music Hall with Milton Berle,” “What’s My Line?,” “The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson,” “The Perry Como Show,” “The Garry Moore Show” and “The Jack Benny Program.” Her dramatic credits include roles on “Maverick” and “Dragnet.”


	In 1952, she signed to an MGM contract, which led to a cameo in Vincente Minnelli’s “The Bad and the Beautiful,” in which she sang on the soundtrack album. She also appeared in “Abbott and Costello Meet the Mummy.”

	Mitch Miller signed her to a long-term contract with Columbia Records, where she made two best-selling albums. She had a string of hit singles, and composer Arthur Hamilton wrote “Cry Me a River” for her but Miller would not let her record the song.

	King starred with Tab Hunter in the television musical “Hans Brinker or the Silver Skates.” She also starred in a TV musical version of “Jack and the Beanstalk” with Joel Grey, Celeste Holm and Cyril Ritchard. She played a stewardess in the 1957 thriller “Zero Hour!” with Dana Andrews and Linda Danell.
	

	She was inducted into the Broadcast Pioneers Hall of Fame in 2010 and was among the first celebrities honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. King’s last released recording was the album “Songs a la King,” released in 2016. She performed regularly in the Philadelphia area, New York and Los Angeles as late as 2014.

	King was born Feb. 16, 1930, to Floyd Henry King and Margaret Finan in Greensburg, Pennsylvania. She graduated from Ravenna High School and sang on radio in Cleveland. She was a regular on “The Mel Torme Show” for CBS and had a successful commercial jingle for Hunt’s Tomato Sauce.

	King is survived by her daughter, Suzy Rudofker, and son-in-law, Dwain Goforth.

title: James Gunn Defends the DC Universe, Says He Dislikes the Idea That ‘Individual Stories Aren’t Meaningful Unless They Lead to Something’
description: James Gunn took to Threads on Saturday to defend the DCU and his decision to expand the universe with “individual stories” amid criticism that his
body:
James Gunn took to Threads on Saturday to defend the DCU and his decision to expand the universe with “individual stories” amid criticism that his films aren’t building toward a major crossover event. 

	Responding to a commenter who pointed out that Gunn doesn’t necessarily need to lay the foundation for one totally interconnected universe, the DC Studios co-head wrote, “I couldn’t agree more.” “DCU is just an alternate universe; we can enter at any location or time and tell THAT story. I dislike the idea that individual stories aren’t meaningful unless they lead to something else. People not understanding this is strange to me, because ‘Star Wars’ has essentially been doing this for 50 years across movies, shows, games and books, admittedly without the tonal variety,” he wrote. 
	

	Gunn pointed out that this approach doesn’t mean there isn’t any connectivity, adding that the “Superman” saga begins with “Superman” and extends into “Man of Tomorrow,” “and contains many characters we’ve introduced in other stories.” “But that doesn’t mean those other stories only exist to set up what’s happening there. I would love people to be seeing ‘Clayface’ because it’s a great, fun horror movie unto itself, not because of where else Clayface will show up three movies from now,” he concluded.


	In the post that Gunn responded to, the user had replied to an image that listed out his DC Universe foundation — “Superman,” “Peacemaker,” “Supergirl,” “Creature Commandos,” “Clayface” and “Lanters” — followed by the text: “What is this building towards???” 
	

	“Clayface,” which his theaters on Friday, is Gunn’s latest DCU installment, following 2025’s “Superman” and this year’s “Supergirl.” (Ahead of the film’s release, comic fans pointed out that the character, who has never been the subject of a standalone feature film, is a considerably nicher choice than previous DCU films.) It generated $24 million from 3,458 North American theaters in its debut, comfortably taking the No. 1 spot at the box office.

	Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star also known as Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan also star. 

	Variety’s Guy Lodge called the film “its own ugly animal; perhaps the characters and conflicts introduced here would pall if given the franchise treatment, but in the context of a single, genre-melding romp, they’re fresh and ickily enjoyable.”

	Gunn’s next film, “Superman: Man of Tomorrow,” hits theaters July 9, 2027.

schema.headline: James Gunn Defends the DC Universe, Says He Dislikes the Idea That ‘Individual Stories Aren’t Meaningful Unless They Lead to Something’

title: Olivia Rodrigo’s ‘You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love’ Returns to No. 1 on Albums Chart Following ‘Expectations’ Remix
description: Following the release of her “Expectations” remix with Chappell Roan, Olivia Rodrigo returns to the top of the Billboard 200 with “You Seem Pretty
body:
Following the release of her “Expectations” remix with Chappell Roan, Olivia Rodrigo returns to the top of the Billboard 200 with “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love,” earning a third total week at No. 1.

	Rodrigo initially released “You Seem Pretty Sad” back in June, bowing atop the chart and remaining there for another week. On October 15, she put out her first-ever remix of “Expectations” with Roan, who also made her feature debut, sending the album back to the top with 75,000 equivalent album units and bumping Taylor Swift’s “The Life of a Showgirl” from the summit.
	

	Zach Bryan enters the chart at No. 2 with his latest “Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs,” which earned 65,500 equivalent album units. It marks his sixth album to break the top 10 and his second release this year following “With Heaven on Top,” which landed at No. 1 in January. “Young Manhood” arrived with just a few days’ notice, touting guest appearances from Lana Del Rey and Turnpike Troubadours and building momentum towards his tour that kicks off in April 2027.

	Elsewhere, Morgan Wallen’s “I’m the Problem” remains at No. 3, while Ella Langley’s “Dandelion” holds at No. 4. Rounding out the top 10 are Noah Kahan’s “The Great Divide,” followed by Drake’s “Habibti” at No. 7, Kahan’s “Stick Season” at No. 8, Olivia Dean’s “The Art of Loving” at No. 9 and SZA’s “SOS,” which returns to the top 10 nearly four years after its initial release in December 2022.

title: Holland Taylor Says She Was ‘Never Paid Very Well’ on ‘Two and a Half Men’: ‘I Got Four Emmy Nominations, and They Never Gave Me a Raise’
description:
Holland Taylor is speaking out about why she didn’t renew her contract on “Two and a Half Men.”

	The actress spent six years as Evelyn Harper, the
body:
Holland Taylor is speaking out about why she didn’t renew her contract on “Two and a Half Men.”

	The actress spent six years as Evelyn Harper, the mother of Charlie (Charlie Sheen) and Alan (Jon Cryer), on the CBS sitcom. She recently revealed that part of the reason she left the show was due to the small paycheck.

	“They never paid me very well on that show. I was paid on that show what I had made on a series like eight years before or something,” Taylor said on the “Alchemy with Anthony Mason” podcast. “And I got four Emmy nominations, and they never gave me a raise. They usually do.”
	

	Taylor was nominated four times for supporting actress during her time on the sitcom. After the sixth season, she declined to renew her contract and instead returned occasionally as a guest star.


	“I stopped being under contract. So, in other words, they would say, ‘Can you do a guest appearance at the end of March?’ And I would say, ‘No, I cannot,’” she said. “I only did it if I wanted to do it.”

	Taylor said the producers were “astonished” by her decision, but she appreciated having flexibility in scheduling.

	“I loved a lot about that show, but they were not full of courtesies,” Taylor added. “In any case, when the six years were up, I said, ‘I don’t want to be on a contract anymore, but I will visit the show occasionally if you want.’ I mean, I did play the boys’ mother.”

	The actress said the team thought she was negotiating and told her they could not afford to pay her more. “I said, ‘You could actually pay me the cost of this building, but don’t bother because I don’t want to continue on under contract,'” she said. “And they said, ‘But we can’t afford to give you more.’ I said, ‘I’m cool with it. I just will come back as a guest from time to time.'”
	

	“Two and a Half Men” ran for 12 seasons from 2003 to 2015. In 2011, Sheen left the show after public struggles with substance abuse.

schema.headline: Holland Taylor Says She Was ‘Never Paid Very Well’ on ‘Two and a Half Men’: ‘I Got Four Emmy Nominations, and They Never Gave Me a Raise’

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Star Stephan James on Paying Tribute to Carl Weathers with His Red Carpet Look: ‘I Can Literally Walk in His Shoes Yet Again’
description:
Stephan James paid tribute to Carl Weathers by donning a white suit on Saturday at the AFI Fest screening of his new movie, “I Play Rocky.”

	James
body:
Stephan James paid tribute to Carl Weathers by donning a white suit on Saturday at the AFI Fest screening of his new movie, “I Play Rocky.”

	James plays the late actor in the Peter Farrelly film, which chronicles the making of Sylvester Stallone’s “Rocky” in 1976. ”

	“This is a three-piece custom King & Bay bespoke suit,” James told me while walking the red carpet at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood. “My friends in Toronto at King & Bay remade this suit for me because Carl Weathers wore the exact same suit to the ‘Rocky II’ premiere in Philadelphia. It was a three-piece white suit, and I had them remake it so I can literally walk in his shoes yet again.”
	



	

					Stephan James at the “I Play Rocky” screening during AFI Fest at the TCL Chinese Theatre on Oct. 24 in Hollywood.
									Variety via Getty Images
	



	The idea came from James’ publicist Samantha Hill. He accessorized with a rose brooch. “Carl had an actual rose, so this is my little twist on it,” James said. “I’m doing something a little more timeless with a brooch.”


	Weathers played fighter Apollo Creed, who fought Rocky Balboa in the first two “Rocky” movies before becoming his coach in the third installment, and died in “Rocky IV” during a match against Ivan Drago (Dolph Lundgren). Weathers passed away in 2024.

	James also told me he had a little chat with Michael B. Jordan after he was cast as Weathers. Jordan played Apollo’s son in the three “Creed” movies. “‘Hey, I’m gonna be your daddy, Mike. I’m gonna be your daddy,’” James said. “So yeah, we had to talk.”
	



	

					Stephan James as Carl Weathers in “I Play Rocky” and Michael B. Jordan as Apollo Creed in 2023’s “Creed III.”
									©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	“I Play Rocky” stars Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone. The film has been earning critical raves — and Oscar buzz — since its premiere in early September at the Toronto International Film Festival.

	The movie, from Amazon MGM, will be released in limited theaters on Nov. 6, followed by a wider release on Nov. 20.

schema.headline: ‘I Play Rocky’ Star Stephan James on Paying Tribute to Carl Weathers with His Red Carpet Look: ‘I Can Literally Walk in His Shoes Yet Again’

title: Hudson Williams Says He’s Writing a Film Featuring an ‘Ex-Hockey Player’ and Is ‘Getting Tripped Up’ by ‘Heated Rivalry’ Parallels
description:
Hudson Williams is working on a new film and is “getting tripped up” over a “Heated Rivalry” parallel.

	Prior to the success of the Canadian queer
body:
Hudson Williams is working on a new film and is “getting tripped up” over a “Heated Rivalry” parallel.

	Prior to the success of the Canadian queer hockey romance that catapulted the actor to fame over the past year, Williams wrote and directed several short films, including “Soakers,” “Buttons” and “Inside Augustine Mendoza’s Quotidian Apartment.” Now, the actor says he is writing a new project where one character is a former hockey player.
	

	In an interview with Entertainment Weekly for “Yaga,” the Canadian witchy detective-thriller Williams stars in, the actor responded to co-star Carrie-Anne Moss’ hang-up over referencing real-life friend Keanu Reeves’ “John Wick” franchise in the show.


	“I’m writing a movie right now, but one character is an ex-hockey player,” he said. “We were like, ‘But if we have this hockey player and then you’ve done a hockey show…’ We’re getting tripped up on it and we’re considering other sports, but for some reason this character just made way more sense being an ex-hockey player. It’s almost like you have to bust through the prison of your own mind or construct of your own mind.”

	The actor did not elaborate on the nature of the project. It’s far from the only thing Williams is currently or recently working on: “Yaga” premiered on Oct. 23, and production began on the second season of “Heated Rivalry” in August. He will also appear in the dark comedic thriller “Apparatus” opposite Dylan O’Brien, and in the ensemble culinary thriller “Tyrant” with Charlize Theron, Julia Garner, Demi Moore and Omar Apollo.

title: ‘Wicker’ Stars Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård and Elizabeth Debicki on Making the ‘Very Silly,’ ‘Really Heartbreaking’ Film: ‘It’s Not Just a Slapstick or Sex Comedy’
description: When Elizabeth Debicki arrived on set for “Wicker,” the first thing she saw was Alexander Skarsgård wading through water — full-frontal. But it was
body:
When Elizabeth Debicki arrived on set for “Wicker,” the first thing she saw was Alexander Skarsgård wading through water — full-frontal. But it wasn’t Skarsgård in the flesh; he was “stark naked as wicker.”

	“I turned the corner, and I was like, ‘Hi, Alex!’ and I went bright red because my brain couldn’t compute what it was seeing,” Debicki tells Variety, sitting alongside Skarsgård and their co-star Olivia Colman in a hotel suite at the Chateau Marmont in L.A. “I was just like ‘Oh my God! Welcome to Budapest, I guess.’”
	

	From married filmmakers Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, “Wicker” follows the relationship between an ostracized fisherwoman (Colman) and her fantastical husband (Skarsgård), who is handcrafted for her by the local basket weaver (Peter Dinklage). When the wicker husband proves to be a better man and partner than the rest of the married men in the village, jealousy erupts, and the unlikely couple must figure out how to preserve their simple life amid the chaos and vitriol. (And yes, Straw-Skarsgård is on full display in the Black Bear film, now playing in theaters.)


	While Debicki needed a moment to grapple with the sight of a naked wicker man, Colman’s reaction mirrored her character falling in love at first sight.

	“It was amazing because we’d all been looking at images for 18 months or so, and then to see it in the flesh, it was amazing,” Colman said. “That [feeling] of, ‘Oh my god, it’s going to work!’

	The Oscar winner was the first to see Skarsgård in his full wicker suit and prosthetic makeup. The prototype had been sculpted after Skarsgård’s features, but when the Weta Workshop artists tried it on someone else in New Zealand, it almost worked, but not quite.
	

	“If it doesn’t quite work, it looks like a horror film because it looks like you cut someone’s face off and glued it onto your own, and that wasn’t quite the tone we wanted to go for here,” Skarsgård explains. “So, it was a lot of anticipation and excitement and a lot of nerves because it was like, ‘Oh shit! If it doesn’t work, then we’re kind of screwed.”

	Thankfully, Colman’s exuberant reaction eased any of Skarsgård’s fears. “It was an incredible day that I’ll never forget. Putting it on and then it helped me find the physicality of the character and then stepping out of the trailer and having Olivia outside going [gasps],” he recalls. “You can see how intricate and how beautiful the work was, and the fact that once it was glued onto my face, it actually moved with my movements. It’s even better than we imagined.”



	

	



	The cast’s multilayered reaction is exactly what moviegoers can expect when watching “Wicker.” The film is intended to warm your heart and make you laugh, but it’s also guaranteed to make you blush. Audiences got their first peek at the film with a steamy three-minute trailer filled with sexual innuendo and hard-as-wood jokes. Since then, the marketing for the Black Bear film has taken on a life of its own, with playful promotional products like hand-woven nipple pasties, a popcorn bucket shaped like the wicker man’s torso and splinter removal kits.

	But the film itself dares to go much deeper. “It’s not just a slapstick or sex comedy,” Skarsgård says. “They did an amazing job with this, and I hope and think and believe that people will go on this journey, be excited with all the twists and turns.”

	In an era of box-office unpredictability, the “Wicker” cast isn’t worried about moviegoers embracing the film’s big swing. The stars believe the fanciful romance’s originality is enough to attract moviegoers to the theater — as evidenced by the post-trailer buzz. “Wicker” captured fifth place with $5.75 million from 1,471 locations, a “strong start” for the low-budget indie, according to Variety‘s Rebecca Rubin. (Black Bear acquired the movie for $2.5 million after it generated buzz at Sundance Film Festival earlier this year.)
	
		The movie is so much fun, but there’s also a lot of serious moments, and a good balance of raw emotional scenes. I wasn’t expecting it to be such a tender love story. How did you establish that balance?	

	Colman: That was all in El and Al’s [Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s] beautiful script. They just got the tone. So, you just had to follow it, and you couldn’t really go wrong. It can be hard to go from very silly to really heartbreaking, but because it was all done with realism, it worked better. 
	

	In my saddest moments in my life, I’ve definitely found myself laughing hysterically as well, which is a very human thing, pain and recovery, all those things. And El and Al just nailed it. It made our journey, our job easier.
	
		What message about marriage and romance do you want audiences to take away from this?	

	Colman: Think wisely. Hopefully, the love you choose enhances your life, not diminishes it.

	Debicki: It’s such a beautiful examination of the idea that loving someone is really looking in a mirror of yourself. You know that’s what’s so frightening. But I always think of the line when Olivia said, “Well, what does he know about love?” And the basket maker says, “Well, I imagine he learned it from you.” That’s what we do in life. We are constantly learning from each other. It’s also a really beautiful examination of the institution of marriage.

	And a lot of this film is looking at what patriarchy does to women, the messaging of women needing to compete. That there’s a kind of scarcity complex that you must do it this way, and she rethinks the system and creates it in the image of herself that’s authentic, and in that she thrives, and that’s a really good conversation to have for women.”



	

					Elizabeth Debicki on the “Wicker” set with directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer.
	


	
		What do you think it says about audiences that they’re willing to come out and root for a wicker husband and a wife?	

	Colman: I think people are excited about something that’s original and different. I think audiences get patronized a bit like, “Oh, they like that film. We’ll do another five like that,” and there’s space for that. But there’s also space for something totally original and different. And El and Al had control of this.

	Skarsgård: The fact that they did have complete creative control and they could have the freedom to make their own movie the way they wanted to make, without lots of chefs in the kitchen or with lots of nervous financiers being like, “Well, are we sure this is going to work?” It was really exciting to be part of that journey. Like we’re making something quite unique here. There’s freedom in that.

	Debicki: We’re in a very difficult time for women. If you look at women in this country and patriarchal systems, a woman’s right to choose what they do with their bodies, and how they live their lives, and just pay disparity in general since the dawn of time. I mean, women rightfully are questioning things, and this movie is refreshing because it’s looking at these issues in a way that’s really accessible and entertaining, but there’s some serious conversations in this movie. I think it’s important to talk about that.
	
	
		People have been having so much fun with their promo and the products that they’re making. What fun merch have you guys been into or seen recently?	

	Skarsgård: We got a splinter removal kit. And those 3D-printed wicker husband torsos. They’re popcorn buckets, and then you fill them with popcorn, popcorn out of like a wicker basket.
	
		What about all the wicker puns? When have we reached the end?	

	Skarsgård: We have a good one.

	Colman: 50 Shades of Hay.

	Skarsgård: It’s been a lot of fun watching this. We all love the film and were very excited when the trailer came out, but you never ever expect that kind of reaction. I’ve never had a movie with that kind of reaction. It’s been really thrilling, and we’re excited to now share the whole movie, more than just those three minutes, with the world.

schema.headline: ‘Wicker’ Stars Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård and Elizabeth Debicki on Making the ‘Very Silly,’ ‘Really Heartbreaking’ Film: ‘It’s Not Just a Slapstick or Sex Comedy’

            The NFL has confirmed they're launching an investigation into Jalen Hurts' medical care and blood clot diagnosis ... after the player was sidelined for the rest of the season.
      
    
            The league confirmed the probe into about how the Philadelphia Eagles handled the diagnosis in a joint statement with the National Football League Players Association Sunday.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Their statement reads ... "The NFL and NFL Players Association are working together to review the matter."
      

            The investigation comes after the NFLPA demanded a full inquiry be made by the league into how his medical treatment was handled.
      
    
            They wrote last week ... "Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred. Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward."
      
    
            As you know ... Hurts was initially diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in his leg ... before the clot spread to his lungs where multiple clots were found.
      
    
            Hurts is now out for the remainder of the season ... and based on what we're hearing, it's imperative he stay off the field.
      
    
            Doctor David Abbasi told Jakson on TMZ's "In The Know" ... the star athlete could be out for 3 to 6 months due to the risk of incurring serious damage from bleeding.
